sections.b: Ignatius wrote to Ephesus from Smyrna, where the Ephesian church had sent its overseer Onesimus, the deacon Burrhus, and Crocus, Euplus and Fronto to meet him (Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:3-2:1; 21:1). It is the longest of his letters. Lake names its aims as those of all the letters but Romans: to thank the church, 'to strengthen respect for the bishop and presbyters', to protest against docetism, and to win help for his church in Antioch. Its best-known lines are 'There is one doctor ... God in man' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2), the stones of God's temple raised 'by the crane of Jesus Christ, which is the cross' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 9:1), the star of 19:2, and 'breaking one bread, which is the medicine of immortality' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:3; Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 9:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2

sections.b:
Lake explains that the letters survive in three forms. The 'long recension' has thirteen letters, the seven Eusebius names greatly interpolated and six more 'clearly not genuine'; the Catholic Encyclopedia dates it to 'the latter part of the fourth century'. The 'short recension' (Lightfoot's 'middle') keeps the seven uninterpolated; Ussher restored it from Grosseteste's Latin in 1644 and Vossius printed the Greek from a Florence manuscript in 1646. The 'Syriac abridgment' that Cureton found in 1845 holds Ephesians, Romans and Polycarp, and Lightfoot 'and others showed it to be merely an abridgment'. The site translates the short recension, as Lake prints it.

In 1910 the Catholic Encyclopedia wrote: 'While it can hardly be said that there is at present any unanimous agreement on the subject, the best modern criticism favors the authenticity of the seven letters mentioned by Eusebius', naming Zahn, Lightfoot and Harnack. Later in the twentieth century the question was opened again. Sergio Zañartu's survey of the recent discussion (Teología y Vida, 2009) names R. Weijenborg (1969), who argued that the short recension was made from the long one; R. Joly (1979), who held the letters a forgery written in Smyrna between 165 and 168; J. Rius-Camps (1980), who kept as genuine only the four letters written from Smyrna; R. M. Hübner (1997), who dated the letters between 165 and 175; and his student T. Lechner (1999). Zañartu quotes W. R. Schoedel (1987), who expected the short recension to remain what 'the scholarly consensus today' sees in it, 'a collection of genuine letters of Bishop Ignatius of Antioch', and C. Munier's survey of a century of research (1993), which found no reason in 'the general opinion of historians and patrologists' to give up the conclusions of the nineteenth-century scholars. Zañartu himself, after weighing the objections, holds to the short recension's authenticity 'until the contrary is proved' (the quotations from his survey are the site's translations). On the other side, B. A. Zuiddam (Ekklesiastikos Pharos, 2010) argues that the seven-letter text may be a medieval abridgment, and that either the whole collection is 'a pious fraud to strengthen orthodoxy of a later date' or eleven letters are Ignatius's own.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2

sections.b: The churches honor Ignatius as a martyr: the Orthodox Church in America on 20 December, as 'the God-Bearer'; the Catholic Church on 17 October, as the memorial of 'Saint Ignatius of Antioch, Bishop and Martyr' (USCCB); and the Episcopal Church and a district calendar of the Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod on 17 October. Their readings of his letters differ, above all on the bishop and on the Lord's Supper (see Ignatius to the Ephesians 6:1 and 20:2 and the cards those notes point to).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 6:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2

common: Ignatius wrote seven genuine letters on his way to martyrdom in Rome early in the second century, in the form Lightfoot called the middle recension. W. R. Schoedel (1987) and C. Munier (1993) called this the scholarly consensus; a few scholars since 1969 have challenged it.
uncommon: The Catholic Encyclopedia reports that the reformer Dallaeus (1666) questioned all seven letters, and that Cureton (1846) held only the three letters of his Syriac abridgment genuine.

sections.h: The one doctor, born and unborn
sections.b: Ignatius sums up Christ in balanced pairs: 'both of flesh and of spirit, born and unborn, God in man, in death true life, both from Mary and from God, first able to suffer and then beyond suffering' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2). Lake prints 'God in man'; the Greek manuscript has 'God come in the flesh' (see the variant there). Either way both sides are true at once, and neither can be dropped.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2; John 1:14; 1 Timothy 3:16

sections.h: Carried in the womb, baptized, made known
sections.b: 'For our God, Jesus the Christ, was carried in the womb by Mary, by God's plan, of the seed of David and of the Holy Spirit' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2). The birth, Mary's virginity and the Lord's death escaped the devil's notice, and were then shown to the world by a star, as 'God was made known in a human way' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1-3). Christ is 'the new man' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:1), 'the Son of Man and Son of God' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1-3; Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:1-2; Romans 1:3

sections.b: Ignatius calls the overseer of Ephesus 'a man of love beyond words' and says that in him he has received the whole church (Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:3). Onesimus came to Smyrna with Burrhus, Crocus, Euplus and Fronto (Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:1), and praised his church's 'good order in God' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 6:2). Eusebius says the letter 'mentions Onesimus, its pastor' (Church History 3.36.5). Lightfoot names him among the bishops the letters attest and adds, 'of the former nothing more is known' (The Christian Ministry, pages 48-49). The letter itself says nothing about his past or his age. Right after naming him, Ignatius writes 'May I always have the benefit of you' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:2), with the rare verb onaimēn that Paul uses in his play on the name: 'Yes, brother, let me gain something from you in the Lord.' (Philemon 1:20). That is a fact of the Greek; whether it points to the same man is the question this page weighs.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:3; Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 6:1-2; Philemon 1:10; Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:2; Philemon 1:20

sections.h: One overseer, a council of elders, deacons
sections.b: Ignatius's letter to Ephesus shows the three-part order: the overseer (Greek episkopos, the word behind 'bishop'), the council of elders (presbyterion) and the deacons. The Ephesians are to be 'submitting to the overseer and the council of elders' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:2); the council 'is fitted to the overseer as strings are to a lyre' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 4:1); there are 'overseers who are appointed throughout the ends of the earth' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 3:2); and 'we ought to look at the overseer as at the Lord himself' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 6:1). In the New Testament the two words can name one office (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5-7). Lightfoot held that the single bishop arose 'out of the presbyteral by elevation', in the regions where the last apostles lived and not apart from 'their influence or their sanction', and called Ignatius 'the staunchest advocate of episcopacy in the early ages'; the Catechism of the Catholic Church takes up Ignatius's picture of the bishop as 'the living image of God the Father' (paragraph 1549), and the Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) reads the same letters as showing that 'the hierarchy of the Church was instituted by Christ'. See the cards at Acts 20:28 and 1 Timothy 3.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 3:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 4:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:1-3; Ignatius to the Ephesians 6:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2; Acts 20:17; Acts 20:28; Titus 1:5-7

common: By Ignatius's time the churches of Asia he wrote to each had one overseer with a council of elders and deacons.
uncommon: Lightfoot argued that the language, 'if taken literally', would give the bishop a 'crushing despotism', and explained it by the crisis of the age.

sections.b: Ignatius names Burrhus, 'my fellow slave', 'your deacon in God's way, blessed in everything', and asks that he stay with him (Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:1). He did: the letter to the Smyrnaeans was written 'through Burrhus' from Troas (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:1). Ignatius calls deacons his 'fellow servants' in other letters too (in Lake's English, To the Magnesians 2 and To the Philadelphians 4).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 12:1; Philippians 1:1; 1 Timothy 3:8-13

sections.b: Ignatius does not use the language of succession from the apostles in his letter to Ephesus, but he ties the overseers to Christ: 'the overseers who are appointed throughout the ends of the earth are in the mind of Jesus Christ' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 3:2), and the overseer is to be received as the one who sent him (Ignatius to the Ephesians 6:1). Eusebius calls Ignatius bishop of Antioch 'second in succession to Peter', and Jerome 'third bishop of the church of Antioch after Peter'. Whether the apostles have successors is the card at 2 Timothy 2:2.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 3:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 6:1; 2 Timothy 2:2

sections.h: The thanksgiving and the one bread in Ignatius to the Ephesians
sections.b: Ignatius warns that whoever is not 'within the altar' 'goes without God's bread' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2), urges the Ephesians to 'come together more often for the thanksgiving to God' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 13:1; Lake: 'It is probable that there is here an allusion to the Eucharist'), and closes with 'breaking one bread, which is the medicine of immortality, the antidote against dying' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2). The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes 20:2 (paragraph 1405). The cards at Matthew 26:26 and John 6 give each church's teaching on Christ's presence in the Supper.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 13:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2; John 6:51; 1 Corinthians 10:17

sections.h: The answer in Ignatius to the Ephesians
sections.b: Ignatius does not name the false teachers at Ephesus, but his answers show what they denied: Christ is 'of flesh', 'born', 'from Mary', 'first able to suffer' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2); he 'was carried in the womb by Mary' and was born and baptized (Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2). Lake's introduction says the letters protest 'against the form of heresy called docetism (dokein), which regarded the sufferings, and in some cases the life, of Jesus as merely an appearance'. The positive teaching is on the page The Incarnation.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:1-2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1

sections.h: Mary's virginity hidden from the devil
sections.b: Ignatius names 'Mary's virginity and her giving birth' as two of 'three mysteries to be shouted aloud, which were done in God's quiet', hidden from the ruler of this age (Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1). Christ was 'carried in the womb by Mary ... of the seed of David and of the Holy Spirit' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2). See also The Incarnation.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1; Matthew 1:18-25; Luke 1:26-38

sections.h: Mary in Ignatius to the Ephesians
sections.b: Mary appears three times in the letter: Christ is 'both from Mary and from God' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2), he 'was carried in the womb by Mary' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2), and 'Mary's virginity and her giving birth' were hidden from the devil (Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1). Ignatius names her to stress that Christ was truly born; he says nothing of her later life.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1

sections.h: Ignatius on the star and the end of magic
sections.b: Ignatius retells the star of Matthew 2 as a light that outshone all the stars, the sun and moon becoming its choir, and says that from then on 'all magic was undone' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:2-3). His word for magic, mageia, is the word family of the magi.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:2-3; Matthew 2:1-12

sections.b: 'A star blazed in the sky, outshining all the stars. Its light was beyond words, and its newness was astonishing. All the other stars, with the sun and moon, became a choir around the star' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:2). Matthew says nothing of its brightness; Ignatius makes it the sign that all creation honored Christ.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:2; Matthew 2:2; Matthew 2:9-10; Numbers 24:17

sections.h: The ruler of this age deceived
sections.b: Ignatius calls the devil 'the ruler of this age' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 17:1; 19:1), building on Paul's 'the rulers of this age' who did not know God's hidden wisdom (1 Corinthians 2:6-8). The ruler's teaching has a 'foul smell' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 17:1); the virgin birth and the cross escaped his notice (Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1); and when the church gathers often, 'the powers of Satan are pulled down' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 13:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 13:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 17:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:1; 1 Corinthians 2:6-8; John 12:31

sections.b: For Ignatius the church's gathering fights in the unseen world: 'when you gather in one place often, the powers of Satan are pulled down', and peace ends 'every war among those in heaven and those on earth' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 13:1-2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 13:1-2; Ephesians 6:12; Colossians 2:15

sections.h: The one doctor and his medicine
sections.b: Ignatius calls false teachers rabid dogs whose bite is 'hard to heal', and then names the cure: 'There is one doctor', Jesus Christ (Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:1-2). The doctor's remedy is the church's one bread, 'the medicine of immortality, the antidote against dying' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2; Greek pharmakon, a drug). The picture grows from Jesus' 'People who are strong do not need a doctor. Sick people do' (Mark 2:17).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:1-2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2; Mark 2:17

sections.b: Ignatius says Jesus 'was born and was baptized, so that through his suffering he might purify the water' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2). Lake thinks the allusion is 'to the Baptism, not to the Passion', and translates 'by himself submitting'. The thought is that Jesus' baptism made the water holy for those baptized after him.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2; Matthew 3:13-17

sections.b: Ignatius calls the Ephesians fellow initiates of Paul, 'who was made holy, who was given a good witness', prays to be found in his tracks when he reaches God, and says Paul remembers them 'in every letter' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 12:2). The verse shows that Ignatius knew Paul as a writer of letters. That he knew several rests on the rest of the letter: its greeting echoes Ephesians 1, and Lake's margin sets 1 Corinthians beside chapters 16 and 18 and Romans beside 8:2, 18:2 and 20:2.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 12:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:1; Ephesians 1:3-14; 1 Corinthians 1:20

sections.b: Early in the second century Ignatius praises the Ephesian church as 'famous through the ages' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 8:1), a church whose Christians 'have always agreed with the apostles' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 11:2), and the road the martyrs take to Rome (Ignatius to the Ephesians 12:2). It had an overseer, Onesimus, a council of elders and deacons (Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:3-2:2), and it had turned away traveling false teachers (Ignatius to the Ephesians 9:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:0; Ignatius to the Ephesians 8:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 9:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 11:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 12:2; Revelation 2:1-7

sections.b: Ignatius wrote to Ephesus from Smyrna, where the Ephesians' delegates found him, and he sends his love to its overseer Polycarp (Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:1). Eusebius says that from Smyrna he wrote to Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles and Rome (Church History 3.36.5-6).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:1; Revelation 2:8-11

sections.b: Ignatius was taken 'from Syria in chains' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:2) and asks prayer for 'the church in Syria', of which he calls himself 'the last of the faithful there' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:2). Lake says one aim of the letters was to secure help for that church in Antioch, where 'the disciples came to be called "Christians"' first (Acts 11:26).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:2; Acts 11:26

sections.b: Ignatius warns of people who carry 'the Name' around with deceit; they are 'rabid dogs that bite on the sly' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:1). Some with 'evil teaching' passed through Ephesus, but the church 'stopped your ears' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 9:1). Whoever ruins the faith by evil teaching goes 'into the fire that cannot be put out', and so does his hearer (Ignatius to the Ephesians 16:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 9:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 16:1-2; 2 John 1:10

sections.h: The Teacher who spoke, and it came to be
sections.b: Ignatius calls Christ the 'one Teacher, who spoke, and it came to be', and says that 'even what he has done in silence is worthy of the Father' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 15:1). 'The one who truly possesses Jesus' word can also hear his quiet' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 15:2). See also The Incarnation.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 15:1-2; Psalm 33:9; John 1:1-3

sections.h: Father, Son and Spirit in Ignatius to the Ephesians
sections.b: Ignatius calls Jesus 'Jesus Christ our God' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:0) and 'our God, Jesus the Christ' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2), yet prays 'through Jesus Christ to the Father' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 4:2). His picture of the church's building joins all three: the Father's temple, the crane of the cross, the rope of the Holy Spirit (Ignatius to the Ephesians 9:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:0; Ignatius to the Ephesians 4:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 9:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2

sections.h: Son of Man and Son of God
sections.b: Ignatius names Christ 'the Son of Man and Son of God', 'who in the flesh was of David's family' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2), and the Ephesians 'members of his Son' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 4:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 4:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2; Romans 1:3-4

sections.b: Ignatius's letter to Ephesus pictures the church as a choir that takes 'God's pitch in unity' and sings 'with one voice through Jesus Christ to the Father' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 4:2), blended with its overseer 'as the church is with Jesus Christ' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:1), and met whole in its overseer (Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:3).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:3; Ignatius to the Ephesians 4:1-2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:1

sections.b: The Ephesians are 'stones of the Father's temple', carried up 'by the crane of Jesus Christ, which is the cross, with the Holy Spirit for the rope' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 9:1), and 'temple-bearers' in procession (Ignatius to the Ephesians 9:2). Each believer is God's temple: 'so that we may be his temples' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 15:3).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 9:1-2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 15:3; 1 Peter 2:5; Ephesians 2:20-22; 1 Corinthians 3:16

sections.b: 'From then on all magic was undone, and every chain of evil vanished' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:3): for Ignatius the coming of Christ broke the power of magic. Ephesus was known for it (Acts 19:18-19).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:3; Acts 19:18-20

sections.h: Prayer for outsiders, and the prayer of the whole church
sections.b: 'And pray without a break for the rest of humanity too, for there is hope that they may repent' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 10:1). The prayer of the whole church with its overseer is stronger than that of 'one or two' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 5:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 10:1; 1 Thessalonians 5:17; 1 Timothy 2:1

sections.b: Ignatius hopes 'to reach the goal of fighting wild beasts in Rome' so as to be a disciple (Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:2), wears his chains as 'the pearls of the spirit' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 11:2), calls Ephesus 'the road that those being killed on their way to God pass along' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 12:2), and offers himself as 'a life in exchange' for them (Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 11:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 12:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:1

sections.h: The church as a lyre and a choir
sections.b: Ignatius pictures the council of elders 'fitted to the overseer as strings are to a lyre', the church singing so that 'Jesus Christ is sung', and every member joining the choir and 'taking God's pitch' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 4:1-2). In 19:2 the stars become a choir around the star of Bethlehem.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 4:1-2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:2

sections.b: Ignatius wrote to Ephesus from Smyrna, 'loving Polycarp' as he loved the Ephesians (Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:1).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2

sections.b: Ignatius asks to be rubbed down with oil, like an athlete, with 'faith, warning, endurance and patience' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 3:1; Lake: 'The allusion is to the preparation of a gymnast or gladiator'), on his way to 'fighting wild beasts in Rome' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:2).
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 3:1; 1 Corinthians 15:32
